# Concert Photo Captions

Generate short social captions that work the artist's own song titles into the sentence as natural wordplay.

## Non-negotiable output requirements

Every finished caption must contain:

1. **The artist's social handle** (e.g. `@iambeckyg`, `@karolg`, `@noahkahanmusic`) rather than their plain name
2. **The venue handle** (e.g. `@lumenfield`, `@tmobilepark`)
3. **The official tour hashtag** where one exists, placed after the caption and before the photo credit, e.g. `#TheGreatDivideTour`. Look it up as part of research. It is a live discovery channel that people actively browse during a tour, and the highest performing post so far was the first one to use it.
4. **Photo credit in parentheses at the very end**: `(📸 @dcongerphoto)`
5. **Emoji, used with intent.** One is fine, two stacked at a pivot point can hit harder when they carry different jobs, like 💚 🌲 for affection plus place.

Formatting rules, learned the hard way:

- **Title Case for song titles, never all caps.** Capitalize the title inside the sentence so it stands out as a title, like "Two green states, one Northern Attitude." All caps gets rejected because the user has to hand-fix it every time, but lowercase makes the reference disappear.
- **No em dashes.** Use periods or commas. Two short sentences almost always beat one long one.
- **Always state the English meaning** of any non-English title, in italics beneath the caption. The user needs to know what they are publishing.
- **Weave the handles into the sentence.** The artist and venue handles should be grammatical parts of the caption rather than tags appended at the end. The photo credit is the only thing that belongs bolted on at the end.
- **Vary emoji placement.** Leading, between the two sentences as a pivot, or trailing before the credit all read differently. Move it around across the options instead of defaulting to one position.

## The formula that works

Two sentences, two or three song titles total. One sentence carries the local or venue angle, the other carries the crowd or performance energy.

Proven examples:

> @iambeckyg came to Arranca, gave Seattle a Shower of hits, and we Can't Get Enough at @lumenfield! (📸 @dcongerphoto)

> She came, she conquered, she reminded Seattle that mañana será bonito. Provenza vibes, Bichota energy. 🔥 @karolg at @lumenfield tonight. (📸 @dcongerphoto)

> @noahkahanmusic turned @tmobilepark into a Vermont field for one night, Northern Attitude and all. 💚 🌲 Seattle sang Stick Season back like We'll All Be Here Forever. #TheGreatDivideTour (📸 @dcongerphoto)

The Noah Kahan one drew the biggest response of any post so far. It is the model to copy: handles woven in as grammar, a long flowing first sentence, paired emoji at the pivot, Title Case titles, a tour hashtag, and the credit last.

Note the first one makes the handle the grammatical subject. That reads far better than bolting the tag on at the end.

## Know who the post is for

Captions are written for a specific radio station's audience, and the station's format decides which chart matters. Ask which station if it has not been stated.

- **Movin 92.5 (Seattle), Top 40 / CHR** is the usual client. Weight song picks by the Billboard Hot 100 and Billboard 200.
- **Country radio** would mean weighting by Hot Country Songs and Top Country Albums instead.

A song that was a monster on a genre chart may mean nothing to a Top 40 audience, and the reverse is just as true.

## Research process

1. **Go straight to the Wikipedia discography page.** `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/<Artist>_discography`, plus the individual album pages for track lists and chart performance. Web search tools have proven flaky and slow for this; Wikipedia fetches are fast and authoritative.
2. **Verify every title before using it.** Confirm the song actually exists and is actually by that artist. Guest features are a common trap: a song may be credited to the opener featuring the headliner, which makes it the wrong choice for the headliner's post.
3. **One anchor hit is enough.** Only one title in the caption needs to be a song the audience would actually know from radio. Once that anchor is in place, the remaining titles can be deeper cuts if the theme or wordplay is stronger. Do not force three hits into a sentence and lose the idea.
4. **Confirm the album title meanings too.** Album names are often better material than song names because they tend to be complete thoughts.

## What makes a caption land

**Ask for the visual first.** The single best caption of this session came from the user mentioning the crowd was dressed in orange and pink, which matched Karol G's song *Verano Rosa* ("Pink Summer"). Details like crowd colors, weather, lighting, and confetti are where the good material lives.

**Use the local angle, but keep it true to the night.** The Emerald City, the evergreens, Lumen Field being the loudest stadium in the world, the 12s, T-Mobile Park and the Mariners. City-specific references outperform generic hype every time.

Never reach for a Seattle cliché that contradicts the actual conditions. Rain is the obvious trap: if it did not rain, a rain pun is just wrong, and the user will notice. Confirm the weather and the vibe before leaning on either.

**Pressure test the reference for legibility.** A caption that needs a footnote has failed. Ask whether a casual listener who only knows the artist from radio can decode it, and name the thing rather than gesturing at it. "Two green states" fails because it never names either state; "Green Mountain State to Evergreen State" works because it reasons for you.

**Mine the artist's own geography against Seattle's.** Noah Kahan is from Strafford, Vermont, a town of under two thousand people, and he called *Stick Season* a love letter to New England. Vermont is the Green Mountain State, Washington is the Evergreen State, and *Northern Attitude* is about a cold northern upbringing while Seattle is the northernmost major city in the lower forty-eight. Parallels like that are specific and defensible, as long as they are spelled out enough to read.

**Look for double meanings.** Becky G's *Arranca* means "start it up," and she was the opening act. The title described the literal situation. Hunt for these.

**Titles that are already English are free wins.** *Shower*, *Can't Get Enough*, *Unstoppable*, *Ocean*. They need no translation and read cleanly to a general audience.

## Traps to avoid

- **Never negate a song title.** Writing "no Stick Season" or "not Homesick" reads first as *the artist did not play that song*, which is the opposite of what you mean and easy to publish by accident. Say "wrong season" instead of "no Stick Season." Keep titles in positive constructions.
- **Verify the handles.** Wikipedia does not carry social handles, so confirm the artist's account separately rather than guessing. A wrong tag is the one mistake that is hard to walk back after posting.
- **Check billing before writing.** Opener or headliner? Never imply an opening act filled the stadium. If two artists share a bill but perform separate sets, do not write anything suggesting a joint performance.
- **Screen for innuendo.** Radio station feeds are brand-safe environments. Becky G's *Sin Pijama* ("Without Pajamas") and Karol G's *Punto G* are both real hits and both unusable.
- **Do not invent attendance figures** unless the venue has confirmed them.
- **Keep collaborations with the right artist.** *Mamiii* belongs in Becky G's post, not Karol G's, since Karol G is the guest.

## Document style

Write the options file as **flowing prose, not a bulleted list**. Explain why each caption works and what the words mean as part of the narrative. The user explicitly preferred this over rigid tables. Lead with a single starred recommendation, then walk through the alternatives conversationally, then close with a short notes paragraph covering what to avoid.

**Every option must be publish ready as written.** Include the handles and the photo credit in all of them, not just the recommended one, so any option can be copied straight out of the file.

**Explain why each individual title works, everywhere it appears.** State what the song is actually about, then say why that meaning fits the shot or the night. This is the user's correctness check, not decoration. It is how they catch a title being used against its real meaning, and it is the part of these documents they value most. Flag it explicitly when a caption bends a title's meaning on purpose.

**Edit the file in place across turns.** Do not delete and recreate it, because that silently drops explanations and options the user wanted to keep.

## File conventions

Save to `photo-social-captions/` in the working directory, named:

```
YYYY-MM-DD-artist-venue.md
```

For example `2026-08-26-karol-g-lumen-field.md`. Open the finished file in VS Code with `code <path>`.
